42	/**
43	 * A {@link Collection} whose contents will never change, and which offers a few additional
44	 * guarantees detailed below.
45	 *
46	 * <p><b>Warning:</b> avoid <i>direct</i> usage of {@link ImmutableCollection} as a type (just as
47	 * with {@link Collection} itself). Prefer subtypes such as {@link ImmutableSet} or {@link
48	 * ImmutableList}, which have well-defined {@link #equals} semantics, thus avoiding a common source
49	 * of bugs and confusion.
50	 *
51	 * <h2>About <i>all</i> {@code Immutable-} collections</h2>
52	 *
53	 * <p>The remainder of this documentation applies to every public {@code Immutable-} type in this
54	 * package, whether it is a subtype of {@code ImmutableCollection} or not.
55	 *
56	 * <h3>Guarantees</h3>
57	 *
58	 * <p>Each makes the following guarantees:
59	 *
60	 * <ul>
61	 *   <li><b>Shallow immutability.</b> Elements can never be added, removed or replaced in this
62	 *       collection. This is a stronger guarantee than that of {@link
63	 *       Collections#unmodifiableCollection}, whose contents change whenever the wrapped collection
64	 *       is modified.
65	 *   <li><b>Null-hostility.</b> This collection will never contain a null element.
66	 *   <li><b>Deterministic iteration.</b> The iteration order is always well-defined, depending on
67	 *       how the collection was created. Typically this is insertion order unless an explicit
68	 *       ordering is otherwise specified (e.g. {@link ImmutableSortedSet#naturalOrder}). See the
69	 *       appropriate factory method for details. View collections such as {@link
70	 *       ImmutableMultiset#elementSet} iterate in the same order as the parent, except as noted.
71	 *   <li><b>Thread safety.</b> It is safe to access this collection concurrently from multiple
72	 *       threads.
73	 *   <li><b>Integrity.</b> This type cannot be subclassed outside this package (which would allow
74	 *       these guarantees to be violated).
75	 * </ul>
76	 *
77	 * <h3>"Interfaces", not implementations</h3>
78	 *
79	 * <p>These are classes instead of interfaces to prevent external subtyping, but should be thought
80	 * of as interfaces in every important sense. Each public class such as {@link ImmutableSet} is a
81	 * <i>type</i> offering meaningful behavioral guarantees. This is substantially different from the
82	 * case of (say) {@link HashSet}, which is an <i>implementation</i>, with semantics that were
83	 * largely defined by its supertype.
84	 *
85	 * <p>For field types and method return types, you should generally use the immutable type (such as
86	 * {@link ImmutableList}) instead of the general collection interface type (such as {@link List}).
87	 * This communicates to your callers all of the semantic guarantees listed above, which is almost
88	 * always very useful information.
89	 *
90	 * <p>On the other hand, a <i>parameter</i> type of {@link ImmutableList} is generally a nuisance to
91	 * callers. Instead, accept {@link Iterable} and have your method or constructor body pass it to the
92	 * appropriate {@code copyOf} method itself.
93	 *
94	 * <p>Expressing the immutability guarantee directly in the type that user code references is a
95	 * powerful advantage. Although Java offers certain immutable collection factory methods, such as
96	 * {@link Collections#singleton(Object)} and {@link Set##unmodifiable Set.of}, we recommend using
97	 * <i>these</i> classes instead for this reason (as well as for consistency).
98	 *
99	 * <h3>Creation</h3>
100	 *
101	 * <p>Except for logically "abstract" types like {@code ImmutableCollection} itself, each {@code
102	 * Immutable} type provides the static operations you need to obtain instances of that type. These
103	 * usually include:
104	 *
105	 * <ul>
106	 *   <li>Static methods named {@code of}, accepting an explicit list of elements or entries.
107	 *   <li>Static methods named {@code copyOf} (or {@code copyOfSorted}), accepting an existing
108	 *       collection whose contents should be copied.
109	 *   <li>A static nested {@code Builder} class which can be used to populate a new immutable
110	 *       instance.
111	 * </ul>
112	 *
113	 * <h3>Warnings</h3>
114	 *
115	 * <ul>
116	 *   <li><b>Warning:</b> as with any collection, it is almost always a bad idea to modify an element
117	 *       (in a way that affects its {@link Object#equals} behavior) while it is contained in a
118	 *       collection. Undefined behavior and bugs will result. It's generally best to avoid using
119	 *       mutable objects as elements at all, as many users may expect your "immutable" object to be
120	 *       <i>deeply</i> immutable.
121	 * </ul>
122	 *
123	 * <h3>Performance notes</h3>
124	 *
125	 * <ul>
126	 *   <li>Implementations can be generally assumed to prioritize memory efficiency, then speed of
127	 *       access, and lastly speed of creation.
128	 *   <li>The {@code copyOf} methods will sometimes recognize that the actual copy operation is
129	 *       unnecessary; for example, {@code copyOf(copyOf(anArrayList))} should copy the data only
130	 *       once. This reduces the expense of habitually making defensive copies at API boundaries.
131	 *       However, the precise conditions for skipping the copy operation are undefined.
132	 *   <li><b>Warning:</b> a view collection such as {@link ImmutableMap#keySet()} or {@link
133	 *       ImmutableList#subList} may retain a reference to the entire data set, preventing it from
134	 *       being garbage collected. If some of the data is no longer reachable through other means,
135	 *       this constitutes a memory leak. Pass the view collection to the appropriate {@code copyOf}
136	 *       method to obtain a correctly-sized copy.
137	 *   <li>The performance of using the associated {@code Builder} class can be assumed to be no
138	 *       worse, and possibly better, than creating a mutable collection and copying it.
139	 *   <li>Implementations generally do not cache hash codes. If your element or key type has a slow
140	 *       {@code hashCode} implementation, it should cache it itself.
141	 * </ul>
142	 *
143	 * <h3>Example usage</h3>
144	 *
145	 * {@snippet :
146	 * class Foo {
147	 *   private static final ImmutableSet<String> RESERVED_CODES =
148	 *       ImmutableSet.of("AZ", "CQ", "ZX");
149	 *
150	 *   private final ImmutableSet<String> codes;
151	 *
152	 *   public Foo(Iterable<String> codes) {
153	 *     this.codes = ImmutableSet.copyOf(codes);
154	 *     checkArgument(Collections.disjoint(this.codes, RESERVED_CODES));
155	 *   }
156	 * }
157	 * }
158	 *
159	 * <h2>See also</h2>
160	 *
161	 * <p>See the Guava User Guide article on <a href=
162	 * "https://github.com/google/guava/wiki/ImmutableCollectionsExplained">immutable collections</a>.
163	 *
164	 * @since 2.0
165	 */

44	/**
45	 * A {@link Collection} whose contents will never change, and which offers a few additional
46	 * guarantees detailed below.
47	 *
48	 * <p><b>Warning:</b> avoid <i>direct</i> usage of {@link ImmutableCollection} as a type (just as
49	 * with {@link Collection} itself). Prefer subtypes such as {@link ImmutableSet} or {@link
50	 * ImmutableList}, which have well-defined {@link #equals} semantics, thus avoiding a common source
51	 * of bugs and confusion.
52	 *
53	 * <h2>About <i>all</i> {@code Immutable-} collections</h2>
54	 *
55	 * <p>The remainder of this documentation applies to every public {@code Immutable-} type in this
56	 * package, whether it is a subtype of {@code ImmutableCollection} or not.
57	 *
58	 * <h3>Guarantees</h3>
59	 *
60	 * <p>Each makes the following guarantees:
61	 *
62	 * <ul>
63	 *   <li><b>Shallow immutability.</b> Elements can never be added, removed or replaced in this
64	 *       collection. This is a stronger guarantee than that of {@link
65	 *       Collections#unmodifiableCollection}, whose contents change whenever the wrapped collection
66	 *       is modified.
67	 *   <li><b>Null-hostility.</b> This collection will never contain a null element.
68	 *   <li><b>Deterministic iteration.</b> The iteration order is always well-defined, depending on
69	 *       how the collection was created. Typically this is insertion order unless an explicit
70	 *       ordering is otherwise specified (e.g. {@link ImmutableSortedSet#naturalOrder}). See the
71	 *       appropriate factory method for details. View collections such as {@link
72	 *       ImmutableMultiset#elementSet} iterate in the same order as the parent, except as noted.
73	 *   <li><b>Thread safety.</b> It is safe to access this collection concurrently from multiple
74	 *       threads.
75	 *   <li><b>Integrity.</b> This type cannot be subclassed outside this package (which would allow
76	 *       these guarantees to be violated).
77	 * </ul>
78	 *
79	 * <h3>"Interfaces", not implementations</h3>
80	 *
81	 * <p>These are classes instead of interfaces to prevent external subtyping, but should be thought
82	 * of as interfaces in every important sense. Each public class such as {@link ImmutableSet} is a
83	 * <i>type</i> offering meaningful behavioral guarantees. This is substantially different from the
84	 * case of (say) {@link HashSet}, which is an <i>implementation</i>, with semantics that were
85	 * largely defined by its supertype.
86	 *
87	 * <p>For field types and method return types, you should generally use the immutable type (such as
88	 * {@link ImmutableList}) instead of the general collection interface type (such as {@link List}).
89	 * This communicates to your callers all of the semantic guarantees listed above, which is almost
90	 * always very useful information.
91	 *
92	 * <p>On the other hand, a <i>parameter</i> type of {@link ImmutableList} is generally a nuisance to
93	 * callers. Instead, accept {@link Iterable} and have your method or constructor body pass it to the
94	 * appropriate {@code copyOf} method itself.
95	 *
96	 * <p>Expressing the immutability guarantee directly in the type that user code references is a
97	 * powerful advantage. Although Java offers certain immutable collection factory methods, such as
98	 * {@link Collections#singleton(Object)} and {@link Set##unmodifiable Set.of}, we recommend using
99	 * <i>these</i> classes instead for this reason (as well as for consistency).
100	 *
101	 * <h3>Creation</h3>
102	 *
103	 * <p>Except for logically "abstract" types like {@code ImmutableCollection} itself, each {@code
104	 * Immutable} type provides the static operations you need to obtain instances of that type. These
105	 * usually include:
106	 *
107	 * <ul>
108	 *   <li>Static methods named {@code of}, accepting an explicit list of elements or entries.
109	 *   <li>Static methods named {@code copyOf} (or {@code copyOfSorted}), accepting an existing
110	 *       collection whose contents should be copied.

112	 *       instance.

114	 *
115	 * <h3>Warnings</h3>

117	 * <ul>
118	 *   <li><b>Warning:</b> as with any collection, it is almost always a bad idea to modify an element
119	 *       (in a way that affects its {@link Object#equals} behavior) while it is contained in a
120	 *       collection. Undefined behavior and bugs will result. It's generally best to avoid using
121	 *       mutable objects as elements at all, as many users may expect your "immutable" object to be
122	 *       <i>deeply</i> immutable.
123	 * </ul>
124	 *
125	 * <h3>Performance notes</h3>
126	 *
127	 * <ul>
128	 *   <li>Implementations can be generally assumed to prioritize memory efficiency, then speed of
129	 *       access, and lastly speed of creation.
130	 *   <li>The {@code copyOf} methods will sometimes recognize that the actual copy operation is
131	 *       unnecessary; for example, {@code copyOf(copyOf(anArrayList))} should copy the data only
132	 *       once. This reduces the expense of habitually making defensive copies at API boundaries.
133	 *       However, the precise conditions for skipping the copy operation are undefined.
134	 *   <li><b>Warning:</b> a view collection such as {@link ImmutableMap#keySet()} or {@link

137	 *       this constitutes a memory leak. Pass the view collection to the appropriate {@code copyOf}

141	 *   <li>Implementations generally do not cache hash codes. If your element or key type has a slow

145	   * A builder for creating immutable multimap instances, especially {@code public static final}
146	   * multimaps ("constant multimaps"). Example:
147	   *
148	   * {@snippet :
149	   * static final Multimap<String, Integer> STRING_TO_INTEGER_MULTIMAP =
150	   *     new ImmutableMultimap.Builder<String, Integer>()
151	   *         .put("one", 1)
152	   *         .putAll("several", 1, 2, 3)
153	   *         .putAll("many", 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
154	   *         .build();
155	   * }
156	   *
157	   * <p>Builder instances can be reused; it is safe to call {@link #build} multiple times to build
158	   * multiple multimaps in series. Each multimap contains the key-value mappings in the previously
159	   * created multimaps.

161	   * @since 2.0
162	   */
163	  @DoNotMock
164	  public static class Builder<K, V> {
165	    @Nullable Map<K, ImmutableCollection.Builder<V>> builderMap;
166	    @Nullable Comparator<? super K> keyComparator;
167	    @Nullable Comparator<? super V> valueComparator;
168	    int expectedValuesPerKey = ImmutableCollection.Builder.DEFAULT_INITIAL_CAPACITY;
169	
170	    /**
171	     * Creates a new builder. The returned builder is equivalent to the builder generated by {@link
172	     * ImmutableMultimap#builder}.
173	     */
174	    public Builder() {}
175	
176	    /** Creates a new builder with a hint for the number of distinct keys. */
177	    Builder(int expectedKeys) {
178	      if (expectedKeys > 0) {
179	        builderMap = Platform.preservesInsertionOrderOnPutsMapWithExpectedSize(expectedKeys);
180	      }
181	      // otherwise, leave it null to be constructed lazily
182	    }
183	
184	    Map<K, ImmutableCollection.Builder<V>> ensureBuilderMapNonNull() {
185	      Map<K, ImmutableCollection.Builder<V>> result = builderMap;
186	      if (result == null) {
187	        result = Platform.preservesInsertionOrderOnPutsMap();
188	        builderMap = result;
189	      }
190	      return result;
191	    }

193	    ImmutableCollection.Builder<V> newValueCollectionBuilderWithExpectedSize(int expectedSize) {
194	      return ImmutableList.builderWithExpectedSize(expectedSize);
195	    }

197	    /**
198	     * Provides a hint for how many values will be associated with each key newly added to the
199	     * builder after this call. This does not change semantics, but may improve performance if
200	     * {@code expectedValuesPerKey} is a good estimate.
201	     *
202	     * <p>This may be called more than once; each newly added key will use the most recent call to
203	     * {@link #expectedValuesPerKey} as its hint.
204	     *
205	     * @throws IllegalArgumentException if {@code expectedValuesPerKey} is negative
206	     * @since 33.3.0
207	     */
208	    @CanIgnoreReturnValue
209	    public Builder<K, V> expectedValuesPerKey(int expectedValuesPerKey) {
210	      checkNonnegative(expectedValuesPerKey, "expectedValuesPerKey");
211	
212	      // Always presize to at least 1, since we only bother creating a value collection if there's
213	      // at least one element.
214	      this.expectedValuesPerKey = max(expectedValuesPerKey, 1);
215	
216	      return this;
217	    }
218	
219	    /**
220	     * By default, if we are handed a value collection bigger than expectedValuesPerKey, presize to
221	     * accept that many elements.
222	     *
223	     * <p>This gets overridden in ImmutableSetMultimap.Builder to only trust the size of {@code
224	     * values} if it is a Set and therefore probably already deduplicated.
225	     */
226	    int expectedValueCollectionSize(int defaultExpectedValues, Iterable<?> values) {
227	      if (values instanceof Collection<?>) {
228	        Collection<?> collection = (Collection<?>) values;
229	        return max(defaultExpectedValues, collection.size());
230	      } else {
231	        return defaultExpectedValues;
232	      }
233	    }

238	      checkEntryNotNull(key, value);
239	      ImmutableCollection.Builder<V> valuesBuilder = ensureBuilderMapNonNull().get(key);
240	      if (valuesBuilder == null) {
241	        valuesBuilder = newValueCollectionBuilderWithExpectedSize(expectedValuesPerKey);
242	        ensureBuilderMapNonNull().put(key, valuesBuilder);
243	      }
244	      valuesBuilder.add(value);
245	      return this;
246	    }

271	    /**
272	     * Stores a collection of values with the same key in the built multimap.
273	     *
274	     * @throws NullPointerException if {@code key}, {@code values}, or any element in {@code values}
275	     *     is null. The builder is left in an invalid state.
276	     */
277	    @CanIgnoreReturnValue
278	    public Builder<K, V> putAll(K key, Iterable<? extends V> values) {
279	      if (key == null) {
280	        throw new NullPointerException("null key in entry: null=" + Iterables.toString(values));
281	      }
282	      Iterator<? extends V> valuesItr = values.iterator();
283	      if (!valuesItr.hasNext()) {
284	        return this;
285	      }
286	      ImmutableCollection.Builder<V> valuesBuilder = ensureBuilderMapNonNull().get(key);
287	      if (valuesBuilder == null) {
288	        valuesBuilder =
289	            newValueCollectionBuilderWithExpectedSize(
290	                expectedValueCollectionSize(expectedValuesPerKey, values));
291	        ensureBuilderMapNonNull().put(key, valuesBuilder);
292	      }
293	      while (valuesItr.hasNext()) {
294	        V value = valuesItr.next();
295	        checkEntryNotNull(key, value);
296	        valuesBuilder.add(value);
297	      }
298	      return this;
299	    }

313	     * Stores another multimap's entries in the built multimap. The generated multimap's key and
314	     * value orderings correspond to the iteration ordering of the {@code multimap.asMap()} view,
315	     * with new keys and values following any existing keys and values.
316	     *
317	     * @throws NullPointerException if any key or value in {@code multimap} is null. The builder is
318	     *     left in an invalid state.
319	     */
320	    @CanIgnoreReturnValue
321	    public Builder<K, V> putAll(Multimap<? extends K, ? extends V> multimap) {
322	      for (Entry<? extends K, ? extends Collection<? extends V>> entry :

351	    @CanIgnoreReturnValue
352	    Builder<K, V> combine(Builder<K, V> other) {
353	      if (other.builderMap != null) {
354	        for (Map.Entry<K, ImmutableCollection.Builder<V>> entry : other.builderMap.entrySet()) {

361	    /** Returns a newly-created immutable multimap. */
362	    public ImmutableMultimap<K, V> build() {
363	      if (builderMap == null) {
364	        return ImmutableListMultimap.of();
365	      }
366	      Collection<Map.Entry<K, ImmutableCollection.Builder<V>>> mapEntries = builderMap.entrySet();
367	      if (keyComparator != null) {
368	        mapEntries = Ordering.from(keyComparator).<K>onKeys().immutableSortedCopy(mapEntries);
369	      }
370	      return ImmutableListMultimap.fromMapBuilderEntries(mapEntries, valueComparator);
371	    }

671	         * and populates currentKey, after which it's never cleared.
672	         */
673	        return immutableEntry(requireNonNull(currentKey), valueItr.next());
